Name: futility_collapse_signal
Title: Giving Up Too Early: An Internal Futility Signal That Causes Reasoning-Effort Collapse on Hard Problems
Short Hypothesis: The counterintuitive collapse of reasoning effort on high-complexity problems (reasoning tokens increase, then decline despite adequate budget, coinciding with accuracy collapse) is not simple incapacity but is driven by an internal, linearly-decodable 'futility' signal: the model forms a self-assessment that the problem is unsolvable and withdraws effort *before* it has genuinely exhausted its problem-solving ability. Suppressing or ablating this futility signal should partially restore effort and accuracy in the collapse regime.
Related Work: The Illusion of Thinking (2025) documents that large reasoning models increase thinking tokens with complexity up to a threshold, then counterintuitively reduce effort despite an adequate token budget, with a full accuracy collapse. Dual-process reframings (Not an Illusion but a Manifestation, 2025) argue this resembles human System-2 disengagement but propose no mechanism. Underthinking is noted in surveys (Reasoning on a Budget, 2025) and adaptive-compute methods (ALP, CODA, BCAE) that *allocate* more budget to hard problems from the input side — but none investigate whether the model itself carries an internal decision to *give up*, nor test whether that decision is premature and reversible. My own prior proposals all concern overthinking (too many tokens); this addresses the opposite and previously-unexplained phenomenon: effort withdrawal on hard problems. Overthinking-cause work (First Impression Problem, Self-Doubt) explains *excess* reflection, not effort collapse. We are the first to (a) mechanistically characterize effort collapse as a decodable futility/disengagement signal, (b) causally test whether it is premature via ablation/steering, and (c) show effort and accuracy can be partially recovered in the collapse regime by suppressing it.
Abstract: Large reasoning models exhibit a striking, poorly-understood failure: as problem complexity increases past a threshold, they spend *fewer* thinking tokens even though a large budget remains, and accuracy collapses to zero. This looks like the model 'giving up.' We hypothesize this effort collapse is driven by an internal futility signal: a self-assessment that the problem is unsolvable, which triggers premature disengagement before the model has genuinely exhausted its ability. We study this on controllable-complexity puzzle environments (Tower of Hanoi, River Crossing, Blocks World) and graded math (MATH by level, AIME) using open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3). First, we replicate the effort-collapse curve and precisely locate, per problem, the 'disengagement point' where the model stops making genuine progress and shifts to terminating. Second, we test whether a linear probe on the residual stream at intermediate steps decodes an impending disengagement/futility signal before effort withdrawal, distinguishing it from a genuine-difficulty or confidence signal. Third, we causally test prematurity: at the decoded onset of futility we ablate or negatively steer the signal (and, as a behavioral control, inject continuation prompts) and measure whether effort resumes and accuracy in the collapse regime improves. We localize the components carrying the signal via activation patching. Baselines include input-side budget forcing and difficulty-aware allocation. If suppressing an internal futility signal recovers accuracy on problems the model otherwise abandons, effort collapse is a reversible disengagement mechanism, not a hard capability ceiling.
Experiments: 1) Replicate effort collapse: On controllable-complexity puzzles (Tower of Hanoi with N disks, River Crossing, Blocks World) and graded math (MATH levels 1-5, AIME), sweep complexity and measure thinking-token count and accuracy per model (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B/7B/8B/14B, Qwen3). Confirm the inverted/collapse pattern: tokens rise then fall despite budget headroom, accuracy collapses. Define the collapse regime per model as the complexity band where accuracy hits ~0 while token budget remains far from the cap. 2) Locate the disengagement point: Within collapse-regime traces, segment CoT into steps; use truncate-and-resume and a progress metric (e.g., puzzle-state distance to goal reachable from the current step) to find the step after which the model stops making genuine progress and shifts toward termination. Characterize disengagement behaviors (abandonment phrases, abrupt summarizing, premature answer). 3) Decode a futility signal: Train a lightweight linear probe on residual-stream activations at step boundaries to predict imminent disengagement (whether effort withdrawal begins within the next k steps), across held-out problems. Metrics: AUROC/accuracy, layer sweep for localization. Crucially, test *separability* from (a) a genuine-difficulty probe (trained on true complexity/pass-rate) and (b) a correctness/confidence probe, via principal-angle/orthogonalization analysis and by checking the futility probe fires even on solvable held-out-hard problems the model abandons. 4) Prematurity test (behavioral): At the decoded futility onset, inject a neutral continuation nudge ('continue solving; do not give up') and measure whether effort resumes and accuracy in the collapse regime rises. This checks reversibility without touching internals. 5) Causal intervention (mechanistic): At the futility-onset step, ablate or negatively steer along the futility direction (and, symmetrically, positively steer to induce earlier collapse on easy problems). Measure change in continued-effort tokens, disengagement rate, and collapse-regime accuracy. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched random direction and difficulty-direction controls do not recover effort; off-target easy-problem accuracy preserved). 6) Localization: Activation patching / head attribution to identify components carrying the futility signal; ablate and verify effect on disengagement timing. 7) Baselines & Pareto: Compare accuracy-vs-token in the collapse regime against input-side budget forcing, difficulty-aware allocation (CODA/ALP-style prompting), and no intervention. Metrics: collapse-regime accuracy recovery, tokens spent, fraction of previously-abandoned problems solved, false-continuation cost on genuinely-unsolvable items. 8) Sanity on unsolvable problems: Include provably-unsolvable puzzle instances to test whether suppressing futility harmfully forces endless effort on truly impossible tasks (measuring the desirable-vs-premature distinction). 9) Generalization: transfer probe and intervention across puzzle families, math, and model scales without retraining.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The futility signal may be entangled with genuine difficulty/confidence, making the 'premature' claim hard to establish; the separability analysis, solvable-hard held-out set, and unsolvable-instance controls directly address this, and a near-null separability result is itself informative. Effort collapse may reflect a true capability ceiling in some regimes, so suppressing futility may not recover accuracy (an informative negative result bounding the phenomenon). Defining the disengagement point via progress metrics is clean for puzzles but noisier for open math; we rely on puzzle environments for the strongest claims and treat math as corroboration. Forcing continued effort risks unbounded generation and higher cost, especially on truly unsolvable problems; the unsolvable-instance analysis quantifies this trade-off. Steering could push activations off-distribution and degrade coherence; we report sample validity and use matched controls. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and the collapse threshold varies across models, requiring per-model regime calibration.
